issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma involving a direct interpersonal assault by a perpetrator with ongoing home-intrusion danger. That is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of witnessed other trauma, where the patient observed trauma happening to someone else rather than being personally harmed.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile is broadly coherent for PTSD with strong links among triggers, threat, appraisals, and memory, but these two items specifically shift the narrative to a victim-of-assault formulation rather than a witness formulation.

vignette:
Dr. Anh Tran, a 77-year-old retired surgeon of Vietnamese descent, still smelled the smoke. He would be standing in his kitchen two years after the operating-room fire, the kettle beginning to whistle, and the heat from the burner would wash across his forearm-a mild, familiar warmth-and suddenly he was back there: the patient's torso a geyser of flame, the sterile drapes catching, the awful crackling. His skin remembered the temperature. He could feel it searing his own arm, even though he was perfectly safe. He would jerk his hand away from the stove, heart hammering, and his wife would look up from her newspaper and ask what was wrong. He would say nothing. These tactile moments were the worst because they came without warning, a simple gradient of heat that bypassed all his reasoning.

General stress also seemed to lower his defenses. On mornings when a mislaid bill or an unexpected phone call from the pharmacy left him feeling frayed, the intrusive images arrived with greater force. He would be trying to balance the checkbook, already annoyed at a small bank error, and the smell of burning flesh would flood his consciousness as though the fire were happening again, right there at the mahogany desk. The emotional intensity of the memory-the horror, the helplessness-was overwhelming, yet the sequence of events remained jumbled. He could not say whether the patient had screamed before or after the flames reached the alcohol prep. What he knew was the raw feeling, as if the memory belonged to someone else, a stranger whose life he was watching from a distance.

In the months after the fire, Anh learned to avoid anything that might pull him back. He refused to watch medical dramas, and when his wife accidentally turned on a news segment about a hospital fire, he left the room without explanation. Certain sounds became impossible to ignore: the beep of a microwave, a car horn, the sudden clatter of pots in the kitchen. Each one made him jump, his palms wet, his eyes scanning the living room for a threat that was not there. And whenever the memory did intrude-the smell, the heat, the screaming-he tried hard to push it away. He would pinch the bridge of his nose and force himself to think of his grandchildren's faces, or recite the periodic table, or simply repeat "Not now, not now" under his breath until the image receded. But the effort itself left him drained, and often, within an hour, another fragment would slip through-louder, more vivid, as if his mind was punishing him for the suppression. He had come to believe that his body was a traitor-an engine that kept revving in neutral, even though nothing was actually happening. "My body is still in the fire room," he told himself. And worse, he began to see this as evidence that something was fundamentally wrong with him as a person. A competent surgeon would have been able to put the memory in order. A competent surgeon would not fall apart at the feel of warm air.

This sense of pervasive danger reshaped his daily life in ways that worried his wife. He stopped wearing his seatbelt, claiming it did not matter. He left sharp knives on the counter within reach of his grandchildren when they visited, because checking for hazards felt pointless when catastrophe could strike without warning. He sped through yellow lights, ignored his own medical appointments, and shrugged when his wife expressed concern. Positive emotions felt especially dangerous. When she brought him a cup of tea and smiled, he would feel a surge of warmth-and immediately push it away, turning his face to the window and concentrating on the sound of the kettle. Allowing himself to be happy seemed like an invitation for disaster. He could not risk lowering his guard.

Six months ago, a fire alarm went off during a routine visit to his eye doctor. Anh dropped to the floor before anyone else moved, breath coming in gasps, hands over his ears. The staff had to help him outside. His wife later found him sitting on the curb, shaking, and insisted he talk to someone. That evening, alone in his study, he admitted he was tired-tired of the constant vigilance, tired of the endless mental pushing-away, tired of feeling defective. He had spent two years fighting his own mind, and the battle was wearing him down. For the first time, he allowed himself to wonder whether trying not to think about the fire was what kept it so close. He was afraid that if he did not get help, he would keep living this half-life, watching the world from behind a wall of vigilance, unable to let anyone in. He wanted to feel like himself again-the surgeon who once trusted his hands. He did not know if that was possible, but for the first time in two years, he was willing to try.

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Dr. Anh Tran, a 77-year-old retired surgeon of Vietnamese descent, lived in a quiet suburban home with his wife of fifty years. For three decades, his hands had performed intricate operations, saving lives with precision and calm. That calm shattered two years ago when he witnessed a catastrophic operating-room fire. A colleague had been preparing a patient for abdominal surgery when a spark from the electrocautery ignited the alcohol-based skin prep. In seconds, the patient’s torso was engulfed, the smell of burnt flesh and singed fabric filling the room. Anh tried to smother the flames with a sterile drape, but the fire had already spread. The patient died on the table. Anh stood in the corridor afterward, his scrubs smelling of smoke, his hands trembling. He told himself he had done everything right, but the smell would not leave his nostrils.

In the months that followed, Anh tried not to think about the event. Whenever an image pushed into his mind—the flash of the flame, the nurse’s scream—he forced himself to focus on something else: the pattern of the ceiling tiles, the feel of his wedding ring. He refused to watch any medical drama on television, and when his wife turned on a news segment about a hospital fire, he left the room without explanation. He began to notice that certain sounds made him jump: the beep of a microwave, a car horn, the sudden clatter of pots in the kitchen. His heart would race, his palms would sweat, and he would scan the room for danger even though he knew perfectly well he was at home. He came to see his body as a traitor—an engine that kept revving in neutral. “My body is still in the fire room,” he thought, “but nothing is happening.” He could not shake the conviction that something was wrong with him as a person. A competent surgeon did not fall apart like this. A competent surgeon could put the memory in order. But Anh could not. The sequences of that day were jumbled: did the patient cry out before or after the flames? He remembered the intensity of the horror—the full emotional impact—but without a clear image. The memory felt as though it belonged to a stranger, not to him. He would sometimes describe it to himself in the third person, as if watching a scene from a movie about someone else’s life.

Driven by a sense that danger could come from anywhere, Anh began to take risks he never would have before. He stopped wearing his seatbelt, telling his wife it did not matter. He left sharp knives on the counter within easy reach of his grandchildren when they visited, because checking safety seemed pointless when catastrophe could strike without warning. He sped through yellow lights and ignored his own medical appointments. When his wife expressed worry, he shrugged. At home, when she brought him a cup of tea and smiled, he felt a surge of warmth—and immediately pushed it away. Positive emotions felt unsafe, as if allowing himself to be happy would invite disaster. He would turn his face to the window, mutter a thank-you, and concentrate on the sound of the kettle instead. He could not risk lowering his guard.

Six months ago, a fire alarm went off during a routine visit to his eye doctor. Anh dropped to the floor before anyone else moved, his breath coming in gasps, his hands over his ears. The staff had to help him outside. His wife later found him sitting on the curb, shaking, and insisted he talk to someone. That evening, he sat in his study and admitted to himself that he was tired—tired of being on alert, tired of feeling defective, tired of a life in which every sound was a threat and every moment of joy felt like a trap. He was afraid that if he did not get help, he would become a danger to himself—or worse, that he would keep living this half-life, watching the world from behind a wall of vigilance, unable to let anyone in. He wanted to feel like himself again, the surgeon who once trusted his hands. He did not know if that was possible, but for the first time in two years, he was willing to try.
